title: Slab-built geometric wall triptych
subtitle: Three linked air-dry clay tiles arranged as a connected abstract wall art piece
excerpt: Three clay slabs are cut to complementary geometric shapes , triangle, rectangle, and parallelogram , and decorated with a consistent incised line pattern before drying. Hung close together on a wall, they read as a single abstract composition. No kiln. No wheel. The hanging hardware is inset during making.
sourceNotes: Geometric wall triptych tutorial for air-dry clay derived from first principles.

content.text: This triptych uses three geometric
slab

tiles cut from the same air-dry clay batch, decorated with a shared incised line pattern, and finished with the same paint and seal. Hanging them close together in a row creates a low-cost piece of wall art that looks made rather than bought.

items.name: D-ring picture hooks or screw eyes

content.text: Make the templates

Cut three card templates: a tall isosceles triangle (base 100 mm, height 180 mm), a rectangle (100 mm x 120 mm), and a parallelogram (100 mm x 120 mm, 20 mm lean to the right). These three shapes work well hung vertically in a row with a 20 mm gap between each. Adjust the proportions to suit your wall space.
Roll and cut the tiles

Divide the clay into three equal portions. Roll each to 8 mm thickness using the rolling pin with slab guides. Consistent thickness is important , tiles of different thicknesses will look mismatched on the wall.
Lay each card template onto the corresponding clay slab. Cut around the template with the fettling knife held vertically. Remove the template.
Smooth all cut edges with a damp finger.
Inset the hanging hardware

While the clay is still soft, press a D-ring hook or screw eye into the top-centre of each tile approximately 15 mm from the top edge. Press it flush so only the hanging ring protrudes. Smear clay around the base of the hardware to lock it in place.
Allow to firm to
leather-hard
before proceeding.
Add the incised line decoration

At leather-hard stage, scratch a repeating geometric line pattern across all three tiles using the needle tool. A consistent pattern that crosses from one tile to the next creates the impression that the triptych is one continuous piece. Keep line spacing even , approximately 8-10 mm between parallel lines.
Smooth the edges of the incised lines lightly with a barely damp finger to soften any rough clay ridges.
Dry, paint, and seal
Allow all three tiles to reach
bone-dry
on a flat surface. Check that the hanging hardware is firmly set and has not loosened during drying.

Apply two coats of paint or coloured slip , the same colour on all three tiles. A dark base with the incised lines left lighter (by dry-brushing a paler colour across the surface) reads well at distance.
Allow paint to dry fully. Seal with two coats of PVA varnish.

items.problem: One tile is thicker than the others
items.solution: Use slab guides (two wooden dowels of the same thickness) under the rolling pin to ensure consistent thickness across all three slabs.

items.problem: Hanging hardware comes loose during drying
items.solution: Pack fresh clay around the hardware base while the tile is still soft, pressing firmly. If it loosened after drying, use two-part epoxy adhesive to re-set it.

Place each tile on a wooden board or sheet of paper and allow to dry away from radiators and direct sun. If a tile curls, place it face-down on a flat surface while still leather-hard and allow to finish drying flat.
